alex: Quick q re: NVTX naming when we correlate nsys timelines with perfetto + KV cache heatmaps. Seeing lots of small kernel switches that make it hard to tell why the kernel selector picked a fallback kernel.

sara: Can you paste the timeline snippet and an example of the NVTX ranges you're using?

alex: pasted a tiny nsys timeline excerpt:

```
Time (ms)   Thread  Kernel
0.00        gpu0    matmul_fp16_q4  (10ms)
10.05       gpu0    kv_prefetch     (2ms)
12.20       gpu0    matmul_fp16_q4  (8ms)
20.50       gpu0    reduce_kernel   (1ms)
```

And current NVTX pushes look like: `NVTX_RANGE_PUSH("kernel_exec")` around the whole request, plus `NVTX_RANGE_PUSH("kv-prefetch")` for prefetch. Not tagging model/version or request id.

miguel: The lack of structured names is the issue. When you have interleaved small kernels, you need a schema so post-processing can group by logical op. I propose a compact convention: `r/<req_short>/<model>/<phase>/<op>`. e.g. `r/7f3b/llama2/infer/kv-prefetch` and for kernels: `r/7f3b/llama2/kernel/matmul_fp16_q4`. That lets perfetto/flamegraph tooling filter by req or op.

alex: yeah that would help. Concern: nvtx strings add overhead and can blow up trace size if we include full model names for every tiny span.

tim: two suggestions: 1) use a short request id (8 hex) in the NVTX string; 2) only emit per-request NVTX spans for spans > X ms or when an error/regression flag is set. For the tiny hot kernels, annotate with kernel variant metadata only (no req id) and include a mapping event at the start of the request: `NVTX_RANGE_PUSH("r/7f3b:meta:model=llama2:v=1:q=4k");` -> then smaller spans can be `kv-prefetch` or `kernel:matmul_q4` and you can join them offline by correlating the meta event timestamp.

priya: +1 for sampling. Also make sure kv cache spans include hit/miss and size. Example: `NVTX_RANGE_PUSH_FMT("r/%s/kv:prefetch:hit=%d:size=%d", id, hit, size)` -- we used `hit=0/1` in a recent perf run and it made it trivial to separate noise from real fetch latency.

alex: example of current exported perfetto annotation after we tried brief naming: "r/7f3b:kv-prefetch" and then anonymous kernel ranges. Still hard to see which kernel selection path caused the fallback.

miguel: Add kernel selector decision range as its own span: `selector:decision:<reason>` e.g. `selector:decision:pad>seq` or `selector:decision:hw_unavailable`. That makes regressions visible in the timeline without adding per-kernel verbosity.

tim: Another trick: use NVTX payloads for small spans instead of long string names (nvtxRangePushA allows a const char* but nvtxRangePushEx supports payloads in some builds). If we pack a short integer tag (op id) and map it in a separate JSON, trace size stays bounded. Not all tools decode payloads though, so fall back to short names like `k:42` and ship `k_map.json` with mapping.

priya: For sampling rules we used: 1/100 req always sampled, and 100% sampled if latency > 300ms or if kv-miss count > 2. That caught a regression where a quantized kernel selector started choosing a lower-quality but slower kernel under certain batch sizes.

alex: Can we agree on a minimal naming set to start? My proposal:
- `meta:r/<8hex>:m/<short-model>:v/<ver>` (one per request)
- `r/<8hex>/kv:prefetch:hit=0|1:size=<N>`
- `r/<8hex>/phase/<enqueue|batch|dispatch|complete>`
- `k:<short_kid>` where short_kid is a numeric kernel id and `k_map.json` maps id->desc (kernel name + arch + qconfig)

miguel: That covers correlation needs and keeps trace strings short. Also add `selector:reason:<id>` events as Tim suggested.

perf-bot: ran quick baseline/patch trace comparison: https://perf.example.local/compare/183305-traces (summary: median tail latency -9%, kv-prefetch noise reduced). :eyes:

alex: awesome. Action items: 1) I will add the `meta` event + short k ids in runtime (PR by EOD), 2) Tim will prototype a small k_map generator during model load, 3) Priya will add sampling config to oncall trace policy.

sara: please also document the NVTX conventions in `docs/trace/nvtx-naming.md` (short page).

alex: noted. thanks everyone :thumbsup:
